scenes.name: hook
scenes.text: Your DTH dish never moves, yet it gets hundreds of channels from space. How?

scenes.name: geo
scenes.text: DTH satellites sit about thirty six thousand kilometres above the equator. At that height, they circle Earth exactly as fast as it spins, so they seem fixed in the sky.

scenes.name: uplink
scenes.text: The TV company beams all its channels up from a big earth station to the satellite.

scenes.name: down
scenes.text: The satellite sends the signal back down over a huge area, covering the whole country at once.

scenes.name: dish
scenes.text: Your dish's curved shape collects the faint signal, and focuses it onto a small device at the front, called the LNB, which boosts it.

scenes.name: box
scenes.text: The signal travels down the cable to your set top box, which decodes it, and unlocks only the channels you've paid for.

scenes.name: rain
scenes.text: In India, dishes point roughly south, toward the equator. Very heavy rain can absorb the signal, which is why the picture sometimes freezes in a storm.

scenes.name: outro
scenes.text: Satellite, dish, LNB, box. TV from space. Follow for more on how things really work.
